new_statements.quote: Stress is contrastive in Koko-Bera and probably also in Kok-Nar and is transcribed acute when attested for a form in either language. [Black 1980:198] ... The fact that length appears to be reflected as stress in Koko-Bera and Kok-Nar could suggest that phonetic stress was positively correlated with length in the protolanguage. [Black 1980:203] ... Contrastive stress accent is generally marked acute (´), but the normally stressed syllable is marked grave (`) where stress has become indistinct (and intonation lowered), typically after the tonic in pronouns and sometimes verbs. [Black 2010:266]

All three quoted passages are present verbatim at the stated locators: Black 1980 p.198 'Stress is contrastive in Koko-Bera and probably also in Kok-Nar and is transcribed acute when attested for a form in either language.' (the 1980 text only shows scanned letter-spacing); p.203 'In Koko-Bera and Kok-Nar length would continue as stress: e.g. *nya:ka-la > KB, KN nákal.. but *panytyi[:]l- > KB pinytyé-' and 'The fact that length appears to be reflected as stress in Koko-Bera and Kok-Nar could suggest that phonetic stress was positively correlated…
new_statements.rule_in_words: For Koko-Bera proper (the language Glottolog equates with Koko Babangk): word stress is contrastive and marked per lexical item (acute), not positionally predictable; it continues Proto-Norman-Pama vowel length, so it can fall on initial, second or final syllables (e.g. nákal 'saw', pinytyé- 'be burning', yukómvrvl 'water fairy'); full vowels occur in stressed syllables, schwa only in unstressed ones; monosyllables show no stress contrast. No statement specific to Kok-Papónk / Koko Babangk exists in anything opened.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Not discussed in any opened source.
new_statements.exceptions: Black 2010: normally stressed syllable becomes indistinct (grave) after the phrasal tonic in pronouns and sometimes verbs; Black 1980: bound-form stress shifts (e.g. pumerír 'father's sister'); monosyllables have no stress contrast.
new_statements.domain_note: Word-level lexical stress, contrasted with a separate phrase-level tonic (one per intonation unit) in Black 2010. Black 1980's Koko-Bera data are Black's phonemicisation of unpublished Sommer field data; Black 2010 is Black's own Kowanyama fieldwork 1977-78. All statements describe Koko-Bera (gugu1254), not the Kok-Papónk variety as such.
new_statements.identity_note: koko1273 is a Glottolog 5.3 BOOKKEEPING (retired) entry: ISO [okg] was created in 2012 on a MultiTree/Bowern request (CR 2011-134) from AUSTLANG Y203 Kok-Paponk, but Glottolog, Black 2005 (abstract: 'a relatively conservative dialect of the same language as Koko-Bera'), Black 1978 and Dixon 2002 all treat it as a dialect of Koko-Bera / Kok-Kaper [kkp] = gugu1254 (already checked; files; Every stress statement quoted here describes Koko-Bera proper (Black's Kowanyama fieldwork and Sommer's data), not the Kok-Papónk variety, whose only attestation is 'limited and problematic data' from one marginal speaker (Gracie Cecil). No source describes Koko Babangk stress as such.

Koko-Bera data = Black's phonemicisation of unpublished Sommer data. No mention of Kok-Pap…

Section 6: 'Black (1978) and Dixon (2002) refer to Koko Babangk as a dialect of Gugubera, Alpher identifies Koko Babangk as a distinct language, though Koko Babangk "is quite probably the language most closely related to Koko Pera" (1972: 68)'; alt names Koko Kunaniy, Koko Baberam; AUSTLANG Y203*. sources.note: p.163: 'The normal position of primary stress, marked acute in this and other words, is maintained in singing only to the extent that it is often made to coincide with the musical beat'; schwa 'occurs only in unstressed syllables'. No positional rule; no Kok-Papónk mention (a full-text search for stress/accent Papónk/Babangk: none).
